title: Celsus likens Jews and Christians to worms
source_text: Μετὰ ταῦτα συνήθως ἑαυτῷ γελῶν τὸ Ἰουδαίων καὶ Χριστιανῶν γένος πάντας παραβέβληκε νυκτερίδων ὁρμαθῷ ἢ μύρμηξιν ἐκ καλιᾶς προελθοῦσιν ἢ βατράχοις περὶ τέλμα συνεδρεύουσιν ἢ σκώληξιν ἐν βορβόρου γωνίᾳ ἐκκλησιάζουσι καὶ πρὸς ἀλλήλους διαφερομένοις, τίνες αὐτῶν εἶεν ἁμαρτωλότεροι, καὶ φάσκουσιν ὅτι πάντα ἡμῖν ὁ θεὸς προδηλοῖ καὶ προκαταγγέλλει, καὶ τὸν πάντα κόσμον καὶ τὴν οὐράνιον φορὰν ἀπολιπὼν καὶ τὴν τοσαύτην γῆν παριδὼν ἡμῖν μόνοις πολιτεύεται καὶ πρὸς ἡμᾶς μόνους ἐπικηρυκεύεται καὶ πέμπων οὐ διαλείπει καὶ ζητῶν, ὅπως ἀεὶ συνῶμεν αὐτῷ. καὶ ἐν τῷ ἀναπλάσματί γε ἑαυτοῦ παραπλησίους ἡμᾶς ποιεῖ σκώληξι, φάσκουσιν ὅτι ὁ θεός ἐστιν, εἶτα μετ᾿ ἐκεῖνον ἡμεῖς ὑπ᾿ αὐτοῦ γεγονότες πάντῃ ὅμοιοι τῷ θεῷ, καὶ ἡμῖν πάντα ὑποβέβληται, γῆ καὶ ὕδωρ καὶ ἀὴρ καὶ ἄστρα, καὶ ἡμῶν ἕνεκα πάντα, καὶ ἡμῖν δουλεύειν τέτακται. λέγουσι δέ τι παρ᾿ αὐτῷ οἱ σκώληκες, ἡμεῖς δηλαδὴ, ὅτι νῦν, ἐπειδή τινες (ἐν) ἡμῖν πλημμελοῦσιν, ἀφίξεται θεὸς ἢ πέμψει τὸν υἱὸν. ἵνα καταφλέξῃ τοὺς ἀδίκους. καὶ οἱ λοιποὶ σὺν αὐτῷ ζωὴν αἰώνιον ἔχωμεν. καὶ ἐπιφέρει γε πᾶσιν ὅτι ταῦτα (μᾶλλον) ἀνεκτὰ. σκωλήκων καὶ βατράχων, ἢ Ἰουδαίων καὶ Χριστιανῶν πρὸς ἀλλήλους διαφερομένων.
pass_a_gloss: After these things, laughing (γελάω) as is customary (συνήθως) to himself, he has compared (παραβάλλω) the race (γένος) of Jews and Christians, all of them, to a string/cluster (ὁρμαθός) of bats (νυκτερίδες), or to ants (μύρμηκες) come out (προέρχομαι) from a nest/hut (καλιά), or to frogs (βάτραχοι) sitting in council (συνεδρεύω) around a marsh (τέλμα), or to worms (σκώληκες) holding assembly (ἐκκλησιάζω) in a corner (γωνία) of mire (βόρβορος) and disagreeing (διαφέρομαι) with one another, which of them might be greater sinners (ἁμαρτωλότεροι), and saying that 'God shows beforehand (προδηλόω) and announces beforehand (προκαταγγέλλω) all things to us, and having left (ἀπολείπω) the whole world (κόσμος) and the heavenly revolution/motion (οὐράνιος φορά) and having overlooked (παροράω) the so great earth, he conducts his commonwealth (πολιτεύομαι) with us alone, and sends heralds (ἐπικηρυκεύομαι) to us alone, and does not stop (διαλείπω) sending (πέμπω) and seeking (ζητέω) how we may always be with (σύνειμι) him.' And in his fiction (ἀνάπλασμα) he makes us closely like (παραπλήσιοι) worms, saying that 'God is, then after him we, having come to be (γίγνομαι) by him, in every way like (ὅμοιοι) God, and all things have been placed under (ὑποβάλλω) us, earth and water and air and stars, and for our sake (ἕνεκα) all things, and they have been appointed (τάσσω) to serve (δουλεύω) us.' And the worms in him say something, we clearly (δηλαδή), that 'now, since some (among) us err/offend (πλημμελέω), God will arrive or will send the Son, so that he may burn up the unjust, and we the rest may have eternal life with him.' And he adds to all that these things are (more) tolerable of worms and frogs than of Jews and Christians disagreeing with one another.
pass_b_english: After this, laughing in his usual way, he has compared the race of Jews and Christians, all of them, to a cluster of bats, or to ants coming out of a nest, or to frogs holding council around a marsh, or to worms holding an assembly in a corner of the mire and quarrelling with one another over which of them are the greater sinners, and saying: “God reveals and announces everything to us beforehand; he has left the whole world and the movement of the heavens, he has disregarded this vast earth, and he lives as a fellow citizen with us alone; to us alone he sends his heralds, and he never stops sending and seeking how we may be with him for ever.”

And in his own fiction he makes us like worms who say: “There is God, and after him come we, made by him and wholly like God (compare Genesis 1:26–28); and all things have been put under us, earth and water and air and stars; all things exist for our sake, and have been appointed to serve us.” And the worms in his account, meaning us, of course, say: “Now, since some among us do wrong, God will come or will send his Son to burn up the unjust, so that the rest of us may have eternal life with him.” And to all this he adds that such claims are more tolerable coming from worms and frogs than from Jews and Christians quarrelling with one another.

choices.choice: object of the comparison moved off 'laughing': 'he has compared the race of Jews and Christians, all of them, to ...' (γένος is the object of παραβέβληκε)
'ants creeping out' to 'ants coming out' (προελθοῦσιν has no 'creeping')
'governs as a citizen' to 'lives as a fellow citizen with us alone' (πολιτεύεται)
'would be more tolerable' to 'are more tolerable' (no ἄν in the Greek)
Genesis 1:26–28 parody checked; Celsus's direct speech kept in quotation marks, Origen's aside 'meaning us, of course' kept outside

Celsus's mocking speeches are in direct first-person form in the Greek ('to us', 'we'), so they stand in quotation marks; the comparisons and the final remark are reported by Origen and are kept as narrative or indirect speech. 'τὸ Ἰουδαίων καὶ Χριστιανῶν γένος πάντας' is the object of παραβέβληκε, not of γελῶν, and is placed so in English. ὁρμαθός (a string or chain) rendered 'cluster', as bats hang together. προελθοῦσιν rendered 'coming out'. ἐκκλησιάζουσι is Celsus's jab at the Christian ἐκκλησία, rendered 'holding an assembly'. 'τίνες αὐτῶν εἶεν ἁμαρτωλότεροι' kept literally: 'which of them are the greater sinners'. πολιτεύεται rendered 'lives as a fellow citizen with us alone'; ἐπικηρυκεύεται 'sends his heralds'. 'πάντῃ ὅμοιοι τῷ θεῷ' and 'ἡμῖν πάντα ὑποβέβληται' parody Genesis 1:26–28 (image, likeness, dominion), cited as 'compare'; the subjection of all things may also recall Psalm 8:6 (LXX 8:7, 'you put all things under his feet'), not cited inline. 'πέμπων οὐ διαλείπει' may recall Jeremiah 7:25 (God sending the prophets unceasingly) and 'ἀεὶ συνῶμεν αὐτῷ' may recall 1 Thessalonians 4:17; both uncertain, not cited. '(ἐν)' and '(μᾶλλον)' are editorial supplements in the copy-text; both are followed, since the sense needs them. 'ἡμεῖς δηλαδή' is Origen's aside inside the report, rendered 'meaning us, of course'. The closing ἀνεκτά has no ἄν and is rendered as a statement ('are more tolerable'). θεός and υἱός in Celsus's parody refer to the God and Son of Christian belief and are capitalised.
